summary:
Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Montenegro since 1977, with an equal age of consent of 14, and no prohibition has been restored. A trans visitor faces no legal exposure for being trans or for presenting in a gender non-conforming way in public.

The Law on Prohibition of Discrimination, passed on 27 July 2010, lists gender identity as a prohibited ground and reaches employment, the provision of goods and services, education and health services. Criminal Code amendments adopted in 2013 and in force from 3 June 2014 prohibit hate speech based on gender identity and provide penalty enhancements where an offence is committed because of the victim's LGBT status, gender identity included.

Those enhancements are applied unevenly. The European Commission has found that prosecutors bring misdemeanour charges where hate-crime proceedings are warranted, which limits the sentencing uplift available in practice.

Legal gender recognition remains tied to invasive requirements. A person may change legal gender only after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and sterilisation, obtaining a medical diagnosis, and divorcing if married. Montenegro had not by November 2025 adopted the Draft Law on Legal Recognition of Gender Identity based on self-determination, after missing its 2024 adoption deadline under the EU accession programme despite completed legislative steps and consultations; no self-determination-based framework is in force.

On relationships, same-sex couples have been able to register a Life Partnership since 15 July 2021, granting almost the same rights as opposite-sex marriage except adoption; Parliament approved the law on 1 July 2020 by 42 votes to 5, and it was signed on 3 July 2020 and published on 7 July 2020. The Constitution bars same-sex marriage, so a trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no marital recognition here. MPs blocked a same-sex partnership law on 31 July 2019 despite government backing, leaving couples without hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights at that time; the Government had adopted a draft partnership law in December 2018 granting near marriage-equivalent rights through a registrar ceremony while explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption.

Organised hostility and state protection appear together in the documented record. The first Podgorica Pride was cancelled in May 2011 after two attacks on gay people in the capital. When the first Pride did march through Podgorica in October 2013, roughly 150 marchers were guarded by some 2,000 police, and rock-throwing opponents were stopped with tear gas. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024, covering 2023, records that anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric continued, and that a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on television was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks, with the police response monitored; more than 222 online hate-speech incidents were reported in the period the review covers.

A March 2012 account describes a small gay scene alongside deeply entrenched anti-gay opinion, with discrimination and harassment when visible. A 2018 ERA study found that 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted; that figure covers LGBT people broadly and its window closed in 2018.
tangentialFactors:
A study cited in the 2024 review found that only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation, a measure of how far workplace protection is written down rather than enforced; the figure concerns sexual orientation and is not broken down by gender identity.

A new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy was adopted with a budget of €45,000, indicating a modest dedicated implementation line rather than a broad protection apparatus.

Gays, lesbians and bisexuals are not banned from military service in Montenegro; the source does not state a rule for trans service members.

Montenegro decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1977, placing it alongside Croatia and Slovenia as a European cohort of that year, which situates the country's baseline earlier than much of the region.

outOfScopeNotes:
This inventory contains no trans-specific killing or violence figure for Montenegro, and none can be derived from it: no count, no denominator and no general homicide rate are supplied, so no comparison of trans risk against background violence is possible here.

Not sourced: how a foreign gender marker on a passport is read at Montenegrin entry, whether any document-marker or visa screening flags gender identity, and whether binders, packers or other gender-related items trigger secondary screening at Podgorica or other ports of entry.

Not sourced: placement rules for trans people in Montenegrin detention or prison, and any visitor access to gender-affirming healthcare or to hormone supplies under Montenegrin medicines rules.

The figure of more than 222 reported online hate-speech incidents is not broken down by target group in the source, so its trans-specific share is unresolved; the same applies to the 28.1% corporate-policy figure, which measures sexual orientation only.

Unresolved: whether the penalty enhancements for crimes committed because of LGBT status have produced completed hate-crime convictions in any period after the European Commission's finding that prosecutors bring misdemeanour charges instead; no case outcomes with dates are given in this inventory.
